draft_evidence.quote: "Seven holds owe me and I owe them. That's the route. I'm at the third, and the fourth is four days on, and it's late already, because I sat at Thornwater for a week and a half with a crew that's not on my circuit." One finger, on her knee. "A crew's walking into a floor where my Path dies. I know what that floor does. I stood at its line eight times alone in the dark to be sure, and I was sure the first time." Two. "The one patient I've never once been able to read is going in first. He says nothing on that floor does anything to him. I've seen it. I've had my hands in him. I still can't read him, and I'm the only healer in a country, and he's going in *first*." Three. "And if I go with you, the fourth hold's another two days late on top of the four, and the fifth after it, and the old woman at the seventh whose knee I did this morning is the same old woman at every hold, near enough, and somebody at one of them might die of a fortnight." Four. She put the hand flat. "That's the whole of it. I've said it all so you've heard it all."

comparison_evidence.quote: Her weighing, aloud, without heat: seven holds owe her and she owes them; a crew is walking into a floor where her Path dies; the one patient she has never been able to read is going in first; if she goes, Thornwater's next visit is eleven days late and somebody there might die of it.

findings.consequence: The first three required considerations are present, but the fourth is replaced with a different hold, a different delay, and a diffuse possible death. This changes the specific cost the packet assigns to Oryn's choice, and 'the old woman at the seventh whose knee I did this morning' also places a Millrace patient at a different route stop without explanation.
findings.repair_target: Restore the packet's specific Thornwater, eleven-day, somebody-there cost in Oryn's four-part weighing and in the route message, while preserving the corrected Millrace geography and all fixed dialogue.

draft_evidence.quote:
She taught him on the road, because she had said she would when the debt was three readings deep and he had one, and because, she said, walking beside him with the mule's rope in her left hand, a road was where she had learned everything she knew about anybody. "Not on a table. Tables are for the hurt. You learn what somebody's *built* like walking next to them. Give me your hand."

"You're asking me."

"I'm telling you. It's my wrist. I'm the one saying yes." She held it out, the right, the coat's cuff pushed back. "You asked at the lean-to and I said no. Now I'm saying yes, and I want you to notice that it's a different day and a different question and that I'm the one who's answering. Put your hand on it. Surface first. Count of ten. Don't go in past the count until I say."

comparison_evidence.quote: On the road south she teaches Cael the reading properly for the first time — on HER, at her direction, her wrist in his hand, consent explicit — and he reads a Tide practitioner's architecture from inside: banks, a channel, a current that runs TO things; 'you're built to arrive' — and she looks at him the way patients look at a diagnosis that is correct. He asked; she said yes; the log records both.

findings.consequence: Oryn explicitly initiates the contact and directs the reading; Cael says she is asking him, but never asks permission to read her. The positive half of the assigned moral checkpoint therefore demonstrates consent without demonstrating his ask-first behavior. The same speech also calls the afternoon road lesson 'a different day' from that morning's lean-to refusal, contradicting the chapter's day-113 continuity.
findings.repair_target: Make Cael ask permission to read Oryn and have her explicitly grant that request at her direction, with the log recording the matched ask and yes; keep both events on day 113 and preserve the refusal as the first test.

draft_evidence.quote:
The lean-to was Millrace's clinic when she was in it and the ford-keeper's drying shed when she was not, and it smelled of both. He catalogued it from the bank's edge, a stride and a half off, which was her distance and had become his: a roof of turf on poles; a plank table on trestles, scrubbed white; the leather roll open on it, its knife and needles and linen in her order; a pan of water going grey; a lantern unlit; a stool she was not using. And the line. Eleven people, when he had counted them, and by the time he had they were nine, because she had done two while he counted.

She worked in the clinical register, aloud, to each of them and to nobody, and the register did not change for the size of the hurt.

The carter's hand first — a crushed thing, the fingers gone the wrong colours, a wheel's work — and she had it between her palms already when they came down, and held it there through the count and past the count, and the man stood with his eyes shut and his other hand flat on the table, and when she let go the fingers were straight and the colours were the colours of a hand, and she said, "Don't lift with it for a week. You will. Don't." That was one. She drank from the pan, not much, and put the pan down, and said, "Next," and the next was a child with a fever, carried, and she put her hands on the child's back and ran the count and said, "That's the chest. It's not in the chest yet. It will be by tomorrow if I leave it," and did not leave it, and the child's breath changed under her hands and the mother's face changed above them, and Oryn said, "Warm, not hot. Water. Send for me if it's back in three days, and it won't be." That was two. An old woman's knee — the old woman, he understood, from a table at Thornwater where the seven holds had been said in order: this was the knee — and Oryn knelt for that one, on the planks, with both hands round the joint, and it took the longest of the three, and when she stood up she stood up as a woman stands who has spent something she keeps count of, and said, "It'll hold to the spring. In the spring I'll do it again. Don't go up the ladder." "I go up the ladder," the old woman said. "I know," Oryn said. "Don't."

Three. Then the dozen small: a split lip, a burn, a boy's wrist that was only sprained, a woman who wanted to be told she was not dying and was told, in the register, that she was not, and went away satisfied because the register did not lie to people. Oryn sat down on the stool for those, and did them with one hand each, and did not use the current on any of them, because they did not need it and she did not have it to spend.

He asked at the eighth.

He had the reading now. It had been awake at contact range for eleven days and he had not once turned it on anyone, and here was the one person on the continent who could show him what a reading of a hurt looked like from the inside, doing eleven in a row a stride and a half from his hand. He asked properly, the way she had told him to, before his hand went anywhere: "The boy's wrist. May I put a hand on it while you do? To feel what you feel."

comparison_evidence.quote: Oryn at Millrace's clinic-shelter (a lean-to with a table) with a line of hold-people: three serious hurts and a dozen small (a carter's crushed hand, a child's fever, an old woman's knee) worked in the clinical register at her reserve's rate.

findings.consequence: Three serious patients plus twelve small patients require fifteen cases, but Cael counts eleven people, the line falls to nine after two cases, and the narration later calls the run eleven. The explicit arithmetic cannot all be true and makes the cataloguing narrator miscount the clinic beat designed to establish Oryn's reserve burden.
findings.repair_target: Reconcile the initial people count, completed-case count, eighth-case placement, and total run with exactly three serious and twelve small cases, accounting for any accompanying caregiver separately.

draft_evidence.quote:
"Here's what I'm not going to do," she said. "I'm not going to join your crew. I've told you that at three tables and I'll tell you at this bank: I don't fight, I don't take a crew's marks, and I've a route, and the route's the only thing I own." She stood up. "Here's what I'm going to do."

She went to the lean-to and took a sheet of the ford-keeper's paper off the shelf and wrote on it, standing, four lines, in a hand he had never seen — square, plain, the hand of somebody who wrote to be read by people who did not read much — and folded it, and went to the mill's door, and spoke to the miller for the length of a count, and gave him the paper, and came back.

"There's a carter going north tomorrow. He'll take that up the route. It says I'm late, and how late, and why, and which hold to send to if the child's chest comes back, which it won't." She picked up the leather roll and put it on her back by its strap. "I've not left the route. I've sent word up it. The holds know where I am and when I'll be back, which is more than they knew this morning. And you're a stop on it. From here. Not the other way round." She looked at Cael. "You're on the route now. Which means when I say lie still, you lie still, and when I say I can't help you, you believe me."

"Yes."

"Then the sixth chair's got a healer in it," Lira said, from the bank, to the ford, "on her terms of service, which is the only kind I've ever seen her offer anyone."

"It's the only kind there is," Oryn said, and went to get her mule.

He catalogued, because it was what he did, that no companion in four years had come on their own terms of service, because none of them had had any: Lira had walked out of an academy, Brom out of a family, Karis out of a ranking, Seln out of a Compact, and every one of them had arrived with nothing to bargain with but themselves. Oryn had a route, and a paper going north on a carter, and a sentence with *when I say* in it twice, and she had put the five of them on her circuit as a stop between the third hold and the fourth and had not once used the word *join*. He wrote that down, at the ford, standing, while she loaded the mule.

comparison_evidence.quote: Oryn does not 'join the crew'; the language is route/stop/terms.

findings.consequence: The outcome is correctly route-based, but Oryn explicitly uses the prohibited join framing and the narration twelve lines later asserts that she 'had not once used' that exact word. The contradiction is audible and draws attention to the very companion-recruitment frame the packet requires the scene to replace.
findings.repair_target: Keep Oryn's refusal and choice entirely in route/stop/terms language so the later catalogue remains literally true, without weakening her service conditions or the sixth-chair outcome.

findings.consequence: The required log text is present, but its assigned fork geography and hours-earlier relationship to the close are replaced with the ford. EXC-B7-003 approves Millrace as the rendezvous; it does not approve deleting or relocating the packet's fork beat, and the manuscript never establishes the ford as a road fork.
findings.repair_target: Stage the fixed log at an actual route fork hours before the ridge ending, or obtain an explicit planning exception that changes the packet's required location while preserving the exact log sentence.

strengths: Worldbuilding is done through mechanism and use. Millrace exists as a functioning wheel, ford, mill, drying shed, clinic queue, carter route, and paper network; healer scarcity is felt through reserve, triage, and delayed visits rather than explained abstractly.

There is no fight, as prohibited. The chapter still contains a memorable noncombat set piece: Oryn uses table, ford, road, note, and route to keep control of her labor. Its win is writable as: Oryn removes the crew's ability to absorb her into their contract by making the crew a stop on her route. At the Stair, ridge, light, sharp boundary, bowl, and rust weathering make terrain load-bearing evidence rather than backdrop.

The refusal is excellent practical trust. Oryn protects the boy from becoming a demonstration, Cael steps back without argument, and Lira's silence supplies the third-party verdict without announcing affection.

Oryn's reserve is made visible through three different treatments, posture, water, changed working method, and refusal to spend current on small hurts. The clinical voice stays blunt and individually useful to each patient.

The architecture-reading image is clear and character-bearing: banks, one channel, and current directed toward contact produce 'You're built to arrive,' which reads as diagnosis rather than theory and gives Oryn a rare moment of being seen professionally.

The final survey sequence is controlled and visual. The bare floor, square stair, boundary stone, duplicate number, different rust depths, and Seln's thumb advance the Compact plant without crossing the line or explaining the site.

All other prohibited outcomes remain absent, names pass the registry ear check, Chapter 17's dialogue close changes to an image close, the chapter is within length tolerance, and all mandated production greps are clean.
concerns: Taste only: the paragraph beginning 'He catalogued, because it was what he did' explains the terms-of-service distinction after Oryn's note and dialogue have already dramatized it. Even after the literal join contradiction is repaired, a later line pass could test whether the scene trusts its objects more.

Taste/continuity only: 'Brom stood with the two mules' ropes in his good hand' can make the previously healed hand sound injured again, while later 'Brom's bow' blurs his established crossbow. The text does not establish a new wound or weapon strongly enough for a verified finding, but the audio read may revive stale state.

Taste only: the clinic's small cases are compressed into a list after the three serious treatments. That is proportionate once the arithmetic is fixed, but the transition currently makes the mandatory dozen feel asserted rather than experienced.
The ask-first refusal, route choice, reading diagnosis, and two-stakes image are all worth preserving intact during repair; they carry the chapter's emotional and structural identity.
